questions.explanation: Conjugacy is orthogonality in the inner product \(x^T Q y\). The Euclidean condition \(d_1^T d_2 = 0\) agrees with it for every direction pair only when \(Q\) is a multiple of the identity. Opposite directions have product \(-d_1^T Q d_1\), which is negative, not zero. Equal images do not make the product \(d_1^T Q d_2\) zero.

\(d_1 + d_2 = 0\), so the directions are opposites
\(Q d_1 = Q d_2\), so the directions have the same image
\(d_1^T Q d_2 = 0\), with \(Q\) the symmetric positive definite Hessian

questions.explanation: \(Q d_2 = (3,\ 2)\), so the product is \(1\cdot 3 + 1\cdot 2 = 5\). The directions are not \(Q\)-conjugate. Reporting \(0\) would be conjugacy, and this pair does not have it. Reporting \(3\) keeps only the first term. Reporting \(2\) keeps only the second. Reporting \(4\) is \(1\cdot 3 + 1\cdot 1\), which replaces the second component of \(d_2\) by \(1\).

questions.prompt: On a positive definite quadratic in \(n\) variables, exact line search along \(n\) \(Q\)-conjugate directions
questions.explanation: The error before the run can be expanded in the conjugate directions. The exact step on one direction cancels that direction's coefficient, and conjugacy keeps later steps from restoring it. After every coefficient is gone, the error is zero. Euclidean orthogonality is not required. Each direction is used once. The first search zeros the gradient along that one direction, not in the whole space, unless \(n = 1\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a long ellipse</title><line x1="28" y1="104" x2="256" y2="104"/><polygon points="256,104 249.6,106.7 249.6,101.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="120" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="104" rx="86" ry="46"/><line x1="54" y1="104" x2="226" y2="104" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="140" y1="58" x2="140" y2="150" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/></svg>

options: needs a further \(n\) steps, because each direction is used twice
stops after one step, because the first exact search already zeros the gradient
reaches the minimizer in at most \(n\) steps, from any start
reaches the minimizer only when the directions are also Euclidean-orthogonal

questions.prompt: Put these steps of one conjugate-direction iteration in order. The directions are already built. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The numerator contains the gradient, so the gradient is computed first. The step length is the quotient of the two quantities formed from that gradient and from the direction, so it comes after both exist. The point moves by the length times the direction, which cannot be formed before the length. Computing the curvature before the gradient would split the second step. The written numerator still needs the gradient, so that split is not an alternative order of these four steps.

steps: Evaluate the gradient at the current point.
Using that gradient, form the numerator as its negative dot product with the next conjugate direction, and form the denominator as that direction's curvature \(d^T Q d\).
Divide that numerator by that denominator to obtain the step length.
Add that step length times the direction to the current point.

questions.explanation:
The product is the first components times \(2\), plus the second components times \(8\).
• \((4,\ 1)\) and \((2,\ -1)\): \(2\cdot 4\cdot 2 + 8\cdot 1\cdot(-1) = 16 - 8 = 8\).
• \((1,\ 1)\) and \((4,\ -1)\): \(2\cdot 1\cdot 4 + 8\cdot 1\cdot(-1) = 8 - 8 = 0\).
• \((2,\ 0)\) and \((0,\ 3)\): both terms are \(0\).
• \((1,\ 2)\) and \((4,\ 1)\): \(2\cdot 1\cdot 4 + 8\cdot 2\cdot 1 = 8 + 16 = 24\).
• \((1,\ -1)\) and \((8,\ 2)\): \(2\cdot 1\cdot 8 + 8\cdot(-1)\cdot 2 = 16 - 16 = 0\).
The first and fourth pairs are not conjugate.

questions.prompt: The Hessian is diagonal with positive entries \(a\) and \(b\). The gradient is \((g,\ h)\) and the direction is \((u,\ v)\). The exact line-search step length equals
questions.explanation: The step length is the negative directional derivative divided by the curvature. The directional derivative is \(gu + hv\). The curvature is \(a u^2 + b v^2\), because \(Q\) is diagonal. Every declared name appears. Dropping the leading minus sign walks the wrong way along a descent direction. Dividing by \(u^2 + v^2\) replaces the Hessian by the identity. Using \(g\) and \(h\) in the denominator, as in \(-(gu+hv)/(g^2+h^2)\), is a steepest-descent length written on the wrong vectors.

questions.prompt: A note claims that two directions are \(Q\)-conjugate. Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The diagonal entries are \(4\) and \(1\), and the directions are the ones stated. The product expands to \(4 - 2 = 2\). Conjugacy requires the product to be \(0\). A product of \(2\) is evidence against conjugacy, not for it. The second term would need to be \(-4\), not \(-2\), before this particular first term cancelled, and that would be a different second component.

steps: Because that product equals \(2\), the directions are \(Q\)-conjugate.
reasons: \(Q\)-conjugacy requires the product to be \(0\). A product of \(2\) means the directions are not conjugate.
\(Q\) is not diagonal with entries \(4\) and \(1\).

questions.prompt: Let \(Q = \mathrm{diag}(3,\ 1)\). At a point where the gradient is \((6,\ 4)\), the direction \(d = (-1,\ 1)\) is a descent direction. What is the exact step length?
questions.explanation: The directional derivative is \(6\cdot(-1) + 4\cdot 1 = -2\). The curvature is \(d^T Q d = (-1,\ 1)\cdot(-3,\ 1) = 3 + 1 = 4\). The step length is \(-(-2)/4 = 1/2\). Reporting \(-1/2\) drops the minus in front of the directional derivative and walks uphill. Reporting \(2\) divides \(4\) by \(2\) in the wrong arrangement. Reporting \(4\) is the curvature.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: During conjugate-direction search, an exact step on direction \(d\) removes the component of the error along \(d\). A later conjugate direction does not put that component back because
questions.explanation: Expand the error in the conjugate basis. The function along one direction is a parabola in that coefficient alone, precisely because the cross terms vanish. The exact step sets that coefficient to zero, and a later direction, being conjugate, has no cross term with which to revive it. A later direction that is a multiple of \(d\) is not a new conjugate direction. The gradient after the first step is orthogonal to \(d\) and is otherwise free. Exact search does not change the given direction into the negative gradient.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 230" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>nested contours</title><line x1="28" y1="118" x2="272" y2="118"/><polygon points="272,118 265.6,120.7 265.6,115.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="204" x2="150" y2="26"/><polygon points="150,26 152.7,32.4 147.3,32.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="266" y="134" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="158" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="150" cy="118" rx="40" ry="24"/><ellipse cx="150" cy="118" rx="72" ry="44"/><ellipse cx="150" cy="118" rx="104" ry="62"/></svg>

options: exact line search forces every direction to be the negative gradient
the cross term \(d^T Q d_{\mathrm{later}}\) is zero, so the later step does not change the coefficient of \(d\)
the later direction is a scalar multiple of \(d\)
the gradient is zero after the first step, so later steps have length zero

questions.prompt: The conjugate-gradient iteration differs from a conjugate-direction run that is handed its directions in advance because conjugate gradient
questions.explanation: Conjugate gradient still takes an exact line search on a quadratic, and the coefficient in the direction update is chosen so the new direction is \(Q\)-conjugate to the previous one. The directions are not supplied as a separate list. They are generated from gradients. A fixed length of \(1\) is not the exact search. Euclidean orthogonality of successive gradients is a consequence, not a replacement for conjugacy. The iteration multiplies by \(Q\). It does not factor \(Q\).

options: builds each new direction from the latest gradient and the previous direction
replaces exact line search by a fixed step of length \(1\)
drops \(Q\)-conjugacy and keeps only Euclidean orthogonality
forms and factors the Hessian at every iteration

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x) = \tfrac12 x^T Q x + b^T x\) with \(Q = \mathrm{diag}(2,\ 6)\) and \(b = (4,\ -6)\). Start at \((0,\ 0)\) and take an exact step along \(d = (-1,\ 0)\). What is the second component of the new gradient?
questions.explanation: The gradient is \(Qx + b\), so at the origin it is \((4,\ -6)\). The directional derivative along \(d\) is \(-4\), and the curvature is \(2\), so the step length is \(2\). The new point is \((-2,\ 0)\). The new gradient is \(Q(-2,\ 0) + b = (-4,\ 0) + (4,\ -6) = (0,\ -6)\). The second component is \(-6\). Its dot product with \(d\) is \(0\), which is what the exact search enforces. Reporting \(0\) is the first component. Reporting \(-4\) is the first component of \(Q\) times the new point, before \(b\) is added. Reporting \(2\) is the step length.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Successive steepest-descent directions are Euclidean-orthogonal under exact line search. That fact becomes \(Q\)-conjugacy for every pair of such directions when
questions.explanation: Conjugacy is \(d_i^T Q d_j = 0\). Euclidean orthogonality is \(d_i^T d_j = 0\). These agree for all pairs when \(Q\) is a multiple of the identity. In that case the level sets are spheres and one exact steepest step reaches the center, so there is no second direction. A general positive definite \(Q\) inserts itself into the product and the two conditions split. A large condition number makes the zigzag worse. It does not turn a Euclidean right angle into conjugacy. The step length is not what inserts \(Q\).

the condition number is large, because a long ellipse makes right angles into conjugacy
the step length is \(1\), regardless of \(Q\)
\(Q\) is a positive multiple of the identity, and in that case one exact steepest step already finishes
